It is certainly possible that $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$ and factoring is easy (ie. can be done in polynomial-time). This belief stems from the mistaken assumption that cryptographic problems are $\mathsf{NP}$-hard problems. An $\mathsf{NP}$-hard problem is one that is hard if $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$. The Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is the stereotypical example. I will come back to this when I talk about ETH. However, no cryptography problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. They are all generally considered to be $\mathsf{NP}$-intermediate2. This means that it is possible that $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$ and all of the problems we base cryptography on are very easy to solve.
  • Even if problems like integer factorization are hard on average, it is not necessary that they be hard for small values like the 128-bit or 256-bit values we often use. This has already been seen in RSA. RSA-512 is broken. We now use something like RSA-4096. It is certainly possible that all our gold-standard theoretical results are perfectly true and these problems only become feasible at something like RSA-$10^{20}$.

what even is a break?

With the above view in mind, let’s focus on a specific cryptosystem: ECDSA.

If the ECDLP (“Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem”) is hard, then ECDSA is secure.

The ECDLP is the computational problem of computing discrete logarithms in elliptic curve groups. There is no need to know what it is in detail: just remember that as far as we know it does not admit a a better than exponential-time algorithm, ie. for a group where each element is of $n$ bits, there is no algorithm that works better than in time $2^{O(n)}$ to solve the problem.

Getting more fine-grained, we have:

If ECDLP is hard, ECDSA has 128 bits of security.

Let’s analyze what this statement means. If a scheme has 128 bits of security, it roughly means that $$\frac{\text{cost of best-known attack (in CPU clock cycles)}}{\text{success probability of that attack}} = 2^{128}.$$

As the equation suggests, it means that you would expect an attack to succeed after spending something like $2^{128}$ CPU operations. An estimate for the number of CPU operations that have ever occurred throughout the history of computing on earth is something like $2\times 10^{36}\approx 2^{120}$. Therefore, if a scheme has 128 bits of security the guarantee you’re getting act the very least is that all the computers that have ever existed combined could not break this scheme in a reasonable amount of time.

There are essentially three ways in which you could attack ECDSA.

  • Break the proof. You could show that there is something wrong with the proof of security, that it seems to omit some kind of fundamental assumption, and therefore that it doesn’t hold. Proofs of security are often wrong. To tell the truth, the statement above is false: no one has ever proved that if ECDLP is hard then ECDSA is secure. The proofs of ECDSA are all in idealized settings like the ‘generic group model’ or the ‘programmable random oracle model,’ and do not correspond to the real world. Therefore it is actually possible to bypass solving ECDLP altogether, and directly attack ECDSA. The proofs tell you what kind of attacks won’t work, but there’s no reason other attacks don’t exist.
  • Find a better algorithm for ECDLP. You could always try to improve the algorithm for ECDLP from exponential to something better. Therefore, attacking ECDLP is a viable strategy, because breaking ECDLP certainly breaks ECDSA.
  • Use a different kind of computer. Suppose I have an algorithm that solves ECDLP in time $2^{72}$, but can actually be massively parallelized. On an 256-core system this algorithm needs each CPU to do $2^{64}$ operations. I set up 32 of these 256-core clusters and put them to work. It would take a single core 150,000 years to do $2^{72}$ operations, but now my new setup would only need to operate for about $2$ years to break an ECDLP instance. These kind of tradeoffs and tricks are extremely common in cryptanalysis. Similarly, perhaps I can come up with a $2^{20}$ time algorithm that uses $2^{64}$ cycles of preprocessing. I simply preprocess once and I am ready to tackle ECDLP as many times as I want. Therefore, you can use ugly computational tricks to break crypto.

This is not even to mention insecure implementations and side-channel attacks, which are also devastating. These are simply the mathematical approaches through which one could break the ECDSA cryptosystem. These breaks can also differ strongly in severity.

  1. A Complete, Complexity-Theoretic Break. A full complexity-theoretic break renders the cryptosystem essentially insecure. For example, a polynomial-time algorithm for ECDLP could classify as a complete break. This is a problem even if the algorithm is too slow to implement on a regular computer—it would mean that we have no theoretical basis for assuming that ECDSA is secure anymore. Furthermore, attacks can only get better. Such a break is devastating.
  2. A Faster Algorithm. A polynomial-time algorithm for ECDLP would destroy the conjectured security of ECDSA. But a faster, non-polynomial time algorithm is still bad. Right now we assume that an $n$-size instance takes $2^{n/2}$ computational steps to solve. To get 128 bits of security, then, we set $n=256$ bits in TLS and use the secp256r1 elliptic curve. An algorithm that reduces the best-known algorithm to $2^{0.0001n}$ would not have any effect on our conjectured complexity-theoretic security of ECDLP. On the other hand, it would almost certainly be able to trivially break the ECDSA protocol used in TLS. To fix this, we would have to set $n=1,280,000$, which would completely change everything about protocol specifications and take a very significant number of man-hours to fix, fundamentally resulting in something that makes browsing the internet far less efficient and compromising numerous of potential devices. Such a break could cause huge problems.
  3. A Faster Heuristic. Suppose that I don’t find an algorithm to break ECDSA. But I find a plausible attack strategy that seems to work well in practice. What happens then? The answer is not great: such strategies, even if not formally breaking anything at all, seem to exist an inordinate amount of time. While SAT (the Boolean Satisfiability Problem) is conjectured to be $2^n$ time in the worst-case, we have very good heuristics that solve the problem. The BKZ algorithm, for example, that is used in lattice cryptanalysis, often uses various heuristics that give it a strong advantage over LLL, which is comparable in broad terms of complexity. BKZ is therefore better on average. Similar heuristics can devastate cryptosystems.

The key difference here is between full breaks and parameter breaks. A full break would essentially leave a cryptosystem redundant: people would simply stop using ECDSA. A parameter break would mean that the scheme would need to be fixed and updated, often in a way that would make it less efficient. Both can cause damage, and both are problematic.

llm cryptanalysis

Where, exactly, do LLMs fit in here?

Current-day LLMs have shown extraordinary capabilities, and can essentially assist (and possibly blow through) every stage of the research process. I’m going to illustrate my point through a number of examples.

1. The Exponential Time Hypothesis

The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) stated that the $k$-SAT problem could not be solved in subexponential time. This hypothesis was disproved by a preprint of OpenAI about a month ago.

This is an exceptional achievement. The algorithm is crazy and difficult and galactic, but it provides the first piece of evidence that we have far less understanding of the theoretical complexities of our algorithms than we suspect. In particular, results have shown that the techniques apply similarly to ECDLP and, more recently, to structured lattice assumptions. This shows the first subexponential time algorithm for ECDLP ever known. Even if this algorithm does not apply to our current parameters, it shows just how little we actually know about ECDLP in the first place.

There is little reason to suspect that this is the only algorithm that LLMs will find. When prompted, frontier LLMs are able to solve exceptional problems, and one of our major heuristics has already been shown to be false. The important thing is that it doesn’t matter if the algorithm is ‘slop’ or if we have no way of understanding it. If we have a way of running it, that is enough. AI has furthermore shown itself capable of solving $3$-SUM and improving on integer multiplication beyond Harvey–van der Hoeven.

2. The HAWK Attack

In July, Anthropic discovered a weakness in the HAWK signature scheme, which produced a (practical) subexponential-time attack for HAWK. The scheme was promptly withdrawn from the NIST PQ-Signature competition. As far back as July, significantly weaker models were able to find major cryptanalytic breakthroughs that had evaded researchers.

Recent AI-assisted breakthroughs have included the quasipolynomial-time heuristic for Classic McEliese (considered the ‘conservative choice’ by cryptographers, whose Goppa-code formulation had been unbroken since 1978 despite years of analysis). Unlike humans, AIs are well-equipped to find such ‘overlooked’ issues: many, many results have involved making such ‘overlooked’ observations. AI is already making cryptographic breakthroughs on the daily: the only reason it is not amenable to cryptanalysis is because the latest models have severely limited cyber capabilities, and refuse to do the task.

3. The Riemann Hypothesis

Levent Alpöge’s recent proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis has been formalized by lean. The proof, surprisingly, appears to use a new algebraic technique derived from the Weil-Deligne proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis over function fields. This uncovers incredible correspondences between various structures in arithmetic geometry, particularly between elliptic curves and automorphic forms. I personally have very little doubt that an AI that can pump out a proof of GRH cannot understand the techniques required to prove bigger theorems in Langlands or BSD. The first time I saw AI do math was in June. If you’re still skeptical, give it another month.

The mathematical ideas here are staggering, and the understanding it brings to the underlying structures of elliptic curves is enormous. Observations far simpler have led to much more significant improvements in questions related to factorization and primality testing.

For example, the AKS primality test reduces the problem of primality testing to polynomial identity testing over a quotient ring. This fundamentally algebraic idea unlocks a new, deterministic, algorithm for primality testing. Similarly, one of the consequences of GRH is that the deterministic Miller-Rabin primality test is polynomial-time. In particular, the original formulation of Miller relied heavily on number-theoretic techniques inherited from GRH. It is not as if GRH has no algorithmic consequences: here’s one, to something immediately relevant to factorization. If there are better algorithms for elliptic curves, there is every reason to believe that an AI that can prove GRH can find it, especially when the machinery used to prove GRH purportedly consists of the following:

Algorithms regularly arise from number-theoretic breakthroughs. The best factorization algorithm for large numbers, the General Number Field Sieve, for example, uses many clever ideas from algebraic number theory. The whole field of isogeny-based cryptography uses complicated algebraic geometry techniques, and the SIDH break uses isogenies between algebraic surfaces.

4. Bootstrapping Practical Attacks

Recently, LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities in making theoretical attacks practical. The following recent work shows that multiple rejected candidates for SHA-3 (some of which had known attacks and some of which didn’t) were bootstrapped by LLMs into practical breaks. For example:

Blender-256 (NIST SHA-3 candidate): Full-round collision resistance had remained unbroken since submission; Earlier models only exploited 64-bit word-size bugs in the C implementation. MIM found those bugs and also broke the underlying construction, finding full-round collisions in 0.36 to 2.3 seconds on a single core.

We have a high degree of confidence in Keccak, but who knows what happens when thoroughly subjected to a superhuman observer? AI has, again, already shown the ability to break 7-round AES as far back as July. Since then, collisions for increasing SHA-256 rounds are posted every day on twitter. While the full 64-round construction is not broken, breaks for round-reduced variants are basically easily findable on regular computers using non-frontier models like GLM-5.3, something previously unheard of. Furthermore, there are easier ways to break Keccak: slight improvements on exponential algorithms for solving multivariate polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is enough, and guess what? An asymptotic improvement to MQ has already been delivered by ETH!

5. Quantum

Many of our cryptosystems, like RSA or ECC, have already been quantumly broken. The PQ-transition has been happening for a while, and AI has shown the potential to significantly accelerate the trajectory of development of quantum computers. While the bottleneck to building quantum computers requires mechanical engineering, theoretical advancements can hugely speed up the quality of engineering required: for example, if one can come up with a small circuit that uses very few qubits and improve quantum error-correction, it makes building quantum computers that much easier.

  1. In terms of Shor, recent AI developments have hugely reduced the number of qubits required to do addition over secp256r1, which is the bottleneck in Shor’s algorithm. Every time this happens, it becomes that much easier for a quantum computer to work.
  2. In terms of quantum computing, AI has made huge advances in quantum complexity, including the recent Aaronson-Ambianis Conjecture and Quantum Parallel Repetition problem.
  3. More broadly, according to Ryan O’Donnell’s exposé of the ETH break, the ETH algorithm is essentially a quantum algorithm interpreted classically. I have heard many remarks from researchers that the field that AI is disrupting most strongly is quantum: even commercially available models have the ability to completely devastate the field and prove several of its most important conjectures.

This is a slightly lower-stakes problem, since we are still at least a couple years away from a working quantum computer able to factor large integers using Shor’s algorithm (or who knows, but this is my guess based on the fact that you still have to physically assemble one, and this is not easy whatsoever).

so what’s the score?

We are now at a situation where:

  1. LLMs have been shown to make generational breakthroughs to both theoretical and practical cryptanalysis.
  2. LLM capabilities are only increasing.
  3. LLMs have been shown to be extremely good at several of the exact things required to break cryptography.

In particular, it is reasonable to assume that the cryptanalytic bottleneck is no longer whether other human researchers have made improbable advances in secret, but rather the actual, physical limits of how good cryptanalysis can get.

  1. It is reasonable to believe that the parameters of basically all schemes are outdated, except perhaps symmetric schemes like AES or SHA. What are the chances we got these correct? Probably not super high—we got everything else wrong. Anything with structure in it can reasonably be inferred to be far less secure than we suspect.
  2. Some schemes are certainly broken. My personal guess is that LWE is going to be the first to go, followed by Keccak. There simply hasn’t been enough work on them. There’s too much structure there that has been unexploited. The study of lattices is nowhere near the level of sophistication as that of ECC—when the AI demon comes, it will find things we’ve never even thought of.

We are no longer at an impasse. We have taken a route, and now we are stuck to it—this is the route where everything is up for grabs and any guesses as to the security of a scheme are flips of a coin. Between the Riemann Hypothesis and AI botnet swarms finding RCEs in everything from PHP to OpenSSL my outlook for the world’s cyberinfrastructure is bleak. The good old days of Ransomware and ZK-SNARKs are gone. See you in a month.

1

Exactly which one of the properties you would have to break for SHA depends on what you’re using SHA for.

2

Sometimes people say that lattice problems like $\mathsf{CVP}$ are $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. They can be, but the actual values for which they are hard are not the cryptographic settings. Trust me when I say that this is not true for the cryptographic versions of these problems.

entry.title: the social reckoning, 1644-1900
entry.content:
One of the general principles through which I approach understanding the current period we are living in (and, indeed, a principle which has yet to prove me wrong) is that we are actually living in a profoundly normal period in human history and our concerns are about as unprecedented as and complex as those of any normal period in human history, insofar the particular amalgamation of things that comprises our current societal problems is essentially as unique as that of any time period: just as the particular set of events that led to the particular assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand can effectively be absorbed into the broader systemic trends of the time which had been whispering ‘mass unrest in Europe’ for quite a while (and not even necessarily in the form of a war, though that was how it eventually manifested), so can our own present situation be understood in terms of the same, complex societal factors that have historical precedent, even if not in the specifics. Of course, anomalies do happen—Alexander happened, and then Caesar (both of them!), then Genghis Khan, and then Napoleon, and so on, and we may yet be on the brink of another historically anomalous situation with respect to the specifics of our overlords, but broadly speaking the manner of this ‘grand societal correction’ that occurs may be anything, but that doesn’t mean it won’t occur nevertheless.

Take technology. Everyone around you will tell you that the march of technological progress is inevitable and attempting to utilize technology as a means to support societal progress rather than adapt societal progress to this inevitable march of technology is foolhardy. This has certainly been true for at least a few hundred years now! Technology becomes increasingly sophisticated, vast numbers of people die or are rendered unemployed, Ellul’s technique spreads its hand over the masses of human civilization, and civilization continues to spread forward and occasionally prosper in tandem with that technology. Of course, these sentiments are motivated not by empirical observation—which would of course reveal this simplicity to be false—but because we happen to be living in the global maxima of technological progress. There is little reason to assume that we have now hit an ever-increasing scale (because the universe and the resources in it are finite, there is by definition no ever-increasing scale, though one would hope that the peak of this particular global maxima arises far, far before we ever hit anything even concerning planetary scales, let alone universal ones) or that technological progress will not inevitably plateau before falling, headfirst, again. Indeed, this plateauing has quite a bit of precedent in human civilization. Here is, for instance, an (incomplete) list of technologies that were widespread within the Roman Empire and yet failed to remain commonplace in medieval Europe after its fall, going so far as to have been subsequently rediscovered even a thousand years after C.E. 5001: concrete, pottery, aqueducts, indoor plumbing, central heating, ceramic tiling, glassmaking, roads, coinage—the list goes on, and the Roman Empire isn’t even the most egregious example of a significant subsequent technological downturn. Take Mycenaean Greece, for instance, which lost writing for about four hundred years after Bronze Age Collapse, or the loss of pyramid-building technology leading to the thousand-year-old question of how did the Egyptians do it, the answers to which have included ‘aliens.’

Similarly, people try to make this argument about how technologies that exist eventually get used, but this is again historically incorrect: human cloning isn’t a thing, people banned CFCs, leaded gasoline, asbestos, laser weapons, etc. Just because they were widespread at some point doesn’t mean that people didn’t retrospectively realized they sucked big time and got rid of them, and it also doesn’t mean that several of the current technologies we take for granted won’t be retrospectively considered similarly barbaric, banned, and people three hundred years from now will wonder how we could possibly have been so stupid to use them so relentlessly.

Of course, just because our problems have historical precedent doesn’t mean that they are not problems, it’s just that this notion of ‘oh my God we are totally doomed forever and we’re going to be living in sci-fi dystopia until the end of time!!’ is a generally hysterical one that isn’t really rooted in any kind of stable framework that involves reality2. But one thing about having historical precedent is that it often lets us estimate how far along we are in terms of such corrections inevitably happening; furthermore, if our knowledge of modern science, anthropology and sociology tells us anything it is that one thing we have actually got a little better at recently is actually doing something to address the societal problems that we have (I wouldn’t say that we’re very good at this, but there have been societies which were quite a bit worse). For example, people recently have been worrying about an AI bubble, which almost certainly exists, and while it is true that as of recent AI-related stocks account for about 45% of the S&P 500, this itself isn’t an imminent sign of the bubble being close to popping3 because railway stocks comprised about 71% of the total UK market in 1848 which isn’t even in the same ballpark, really.

old man sorkin

All that preamble I didn’t even arrive at the second core thesis of my general line of reasoning, which is that all politics is essentially a materialist politics. This will make more sense in due course, once I make my way through why I’m thinking about this kind of technological determinism in the first place: it’s spurred, unfortunately, by a Friday-night viewing of Aaron Sorkin’s new film The Social Reckoning, which is supposed to be a spiritual sequel to his and Fincher’s 2011 masterpiece The Social Network. Unfortunately The Social Reckoning is much more of a literal sequel to The Social Network than a spiritual one. Fincher’s movie is really really good. Sorkin’s new film is pretty awful. And this isn’t even because of Mikey Madison and Jeremy Allen White (both of whom I find myself always determined to hate but ultimately do find pleasant on screen) but because Sorkin’s ‘sauce’ which has always been flavored with a little bit of a preachy and distracting utopian liberalism has finally been lost which means that the neoliberalism is all that remains. I always think back to the old Truffaut take of how there are no anti-war films because cinema glorifies whatever it displays by making it look pretty and heightened4 when I think of biopics—they, too, can’t help but glorify their subject—and how this new onslaught of tech biopics we’re getting these days (Zuckerberg, Altman, Elizabeth Holmes, SBF, ugh) are going to deal with the problem of accidentally rehabilitating the most reprehensible drug-addled lizards on Earth by making them look actually interesting through giving them a highlight in the form of movie instead of like the mind-numbingly boring lizards that they are in real life5. Sorkin’s approach is to make Zuck look and feel like a Bond villain while Bill Burr screams at him. There’s also this scene where Jan 6th is going on and everyone’s looking at Zuck asking him to personally delete the Facebook livestream in the ‘war room’ which openly advocates for the fact that Facebook should basically regulate the content on their platform, a really beautiful can of worms only Aaron Sorkin could serve to you on a platter because of Newsroom-era insistence that the institutions of American politics are wonderful, it’s just the people in them who suck, as if it weren’t the case that the institutions—inbuilt with a complex system of checks and balances—were successively weakened over the years in a deliberate attempt to reduce corporate regulation and consolidate executive power6.

Anyway, this movie sucks and is saved to some extent by the fact that Mikey Madison is both pretty and pretty great in it, and also because it’s generally fun to watch. Setting aside Sorkin’s stupid insistence that Facebook needs to start regulating the content on its platform7, however, is the more important question of what is to be done. Here is a technology that has intensely negative impacts on both mental health and the health of political discourse in a country, is essentially one of the most successful mass surveillance mechanisms of all time, algorithmically radicalizes the masses into consumerism and political negligence, somehow has also been linked with declining birth rates, of all things, makes people stupider and destroys their attention spans, carries with it all the negative consequences of television that better writers like DFW or Baudrillard have pointed out already ad nauseam, and also, as per Sam Kriss, serves as a refuge for demons:

The internet is not a communications system. Instead of delivering messages between people, it simulates the experience of being among people, in a way that books or shopping lists or even the telephone do not. And there are things that a simulation will always fail to capture. In the philosophy of Emmanuel Lévinas, your ethical responsibility to other people emerges out of their face, the experience of looking directly into the face of another living subject. “The face is what prohibits us from killing.” Elsewhere: “The human face is the conduit for the word of God.” But Facebook is a world without faces. Only images of faces; selfies, avatars: dead things. Or the moving image in a FaceTime chat: a haunted puppet. There is always something in the way. You are not talking to a person: the machine is talking, through you, to itself.

Provocative and essentially correct, but what I am drawn to is this later section from his sequel article The Internet is Already Over:

In the future—not the distant future, but ten years, five—people will remember the internet as a brief dumb enthusiasm, like phrenology or the dirigible. They might still use computer networks to send an email or manage their bank accounts, but those networks will not be where culture or politics happens. The idea of spending all day online will seem as ridiculous as sitting down in front of a nice fire to read the phone book. Soon, people will find it incredible that for several decades all our art was obsessed with digital computers: all those novels and films and exhibitions about tin cans that make beeping noises, handy if you need to multiply two big numbers together, but so lifeless, so sexless, so grey synthetic glassy bugeyed spreadsheet plastic drab. And all your smug chortling over the people who failed to predict our internetty present—if anyone remembers it, it’ll be with exactly the same laugh.

Kriss wrote this in 2022. Five years is perhaps too eerily prescient to be true, but the ten years is looking like an inevitability at this point: and it comes out of not some kind of public push towards increasing mass morality, but through the eventual transformation of the internet into the kind of ‘agentic wasteland’ which renders it essentially obsolete. Ultimately, the facade of social media is that humans are interacting with humans; interacting with non-humans via such mechanisms carries no such appeal. Bots have already rid myself of my own social media existence, which remains limited to, say, 20 mins a day of Instagram (although if you count messaging apps as social media then that’s a different thing altogether—I do spend a lot of time talking to real people over the internet) and recent grumbles from my parents about LLM-generated content flooding the mainstream and causing misunderstandings to outright cyberattacks seems to point towards a promising endpoint of the internet being essentially unusable in any social or even information-receiving capacity, with made-up news becoming more of an algorithmic frenzy than ever; people will soon only be able to pay attention to the things that happen locally, physically around them, because the only things that are real, of course—even while the internet was going on well and good—were those that happened in front of your own eyes.

Ultimately the distinction to me remains that AI and the internet are fundamentally the same thing: the embodiment of the emergent human consciousness, and while it used to be run by humans themselves they’ve now given a name and a face to it and seem to be selling it as super-intelligence8.

neoliberal accelerator

There is a scientific sense in which AI and the internet are not the same thing: informally speaking you can categorize new forms of technology into technologies of efficiency and technologies of power, and the differences in how they affect society stems from the ways they manifest as technologies of power.

Take the mass spectrometer. This is a device that is used to measure the mass-to-charge ratio of particles. The mass spectrometer is a staple instrument of chemists because it fundamentally does something that human beings cannot do: no amount of human intellectual capability or effort can result in the kind of precision that a mass spectrometer provides, and in doing so it provides humans a qualitatively new way of doing a particular thing—in this case, measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of particles. The nuclear bomb is also such a technology of power, because it enables the kind of mass destruction that is otherwise impossible for a human being to accomplish. So is the lightbulb, or the microwave, or the refrigerator, or contraceptives, or pasteurization. These technologies enable human beings to do something that they qualitatively were unable to do before. They fundamentally create something new.

This is not what the internet is, or what the car is. These are primarily technologies of efficiency: they allow humans to do something in a much faster and more efficient manner—communication and transportation, namely. LLMs, similarly, are technologies of acceleration: fundamentally they mimic human cognitive behavior, they just do it at scale and very quickly. Because of the efficiency with which these things process collective human tasks they make it possible to monetize certain metrics of human social behavior that otherwise remains natural. For example, I can always talk to my friend for free, but if I want to do it right now and from anywhere on earth and as fast as possible you can charge me a fee to do that. Of course, the resulting transaction is merely a simulation of the social desire I possessed—in reality I am not talking to my friend over the telephone, I am merely communicating with the actual phone itself, which is repeating the words my friend says. What the telephone does in this sense is decouple the act of socialization with the act of communication. To talk to my friend I ordinarily need to perform the necessary social rituals; shake his hand, perhaps, or dress to some inordinate degree—I need to do none of these things over the phone, and so the manner of communication is different. Talking over the phone is a conversation consisting of merely relaying information to each other—it does not take advantage of the shared social and physical environment you both inhabit, or your surroundings, or the natural friction of co-inhabited spaces. In some sense, it is a lot more like quickly scribbling letters to each other—which is, in fact, what texting is.

This decoupling of social rituals with the actual phenomenon of communication has interesting effects. For example, it is well-known that people are more likely to be flaky when they have the option of quick communication—it is a lot easier to cancel on someone than to not turn up and suffer the social consequences of making them wait, which is a significant inconvenience on your part. Socially, the internet and LLMs push this a step further: they decouple the already-weakened socialization of telephone calls with mere simulation of conversation, eliminating any of the social friction required to keep even a telephone call sustainable (the requirement of saying “Hello,” for instance, or the implicit knowledge that the person you are talking to you have a relationship with outside the telephone and therefore could potentially suffer consequences for when it comes to the violation of a social contract). In this way it is possible to pepper over the natural consequences of human interaction that lead to reductions in productivity and instead achieve a wholehearted society of efficiency through the use of social engineering technologies.

People didn’t have anyone to talk to at home, so they used to know their neighbors: now you can talk to whoever you want, so there’s no need to!

Of course, the meaningful hit here is terms of the quality of life of the actual human beings involved, but neoliberal thought considers humans to be secondary to the optimization activity of production and capital accumulation. In this sense, LLMs when viewed as social or efficiency technologies are essentially technologies that decouple the human activities of scientific thought with the accumulation of scientific results, because scientific results are gameable: you can make money off harnessing lightning, but you can’t make money off the intellectual phenomenon of the enlightenment which was equally guided by scientific thought! This phenomenon of neoliberal acceleration essentially seeks to eliminate all human intellectual and spiritual achievement and turn humanity into something Borg-like, concerned primarily with efficiency or technique above all costs.

This is all well and good, if not for several basic scientific observations that render the neoliberal dream dead in the water:

  1. Humans are sustainable. Essentially all the resources required to maintain human civilization at a base scale are renewable. You can grow food and trees. You cannot produce cobalt out of nowhere—once it’s run out, it’s run out, and then you can’t make batteries anymore.
  2. Humans have an extraordinary amount of collective power. If you render the masses extremely unhappy, they will kill you.
  3. The cognitive rewiring that social engineering technologies do make them effectively unsustainable. Social media derangement leads to bizarre and incoherent political ideologies that fracture the whole concept of politics in the first place. LLM use makes people stupid and incapable at performing tasks without LLMs, which renders them unable to fix problems caused by the aforementioned LLMs9.

Nevertheless, it is not true that these things cannot cause mass harm! The conclusion is that the neoliberal dream does not really have any kind of logical ending beyond an unsustainable equilibrium of feudalism10, and the question is exactly how far these new AI technologies take along that road.

And just as it took us 20 years to realize that the internet was essentially a bit of a crockpot, so do I think it will take us another 40, maybe 50 at most before all these things: social media hallucinations, LLM psychosis—these things go away. They will not be around forever, no matter what people tell you. This is the real world, not some kind of psychological playground. Either people learn to live sustainably with social media in a way that it actively enhances the quality of life of the citizens of the world—or at the very least the downside does not result in fertility decline so severe that the human race becomes incapable of propagating—or it will be banned. They will get rid of it.

It seems inconceivable. But, as every historical event has precedent, so does this one.

the chinese opioid crisis

In 1799 the Qing empire banned opium importation. Over the past 100 years, opium in China had grown from being a medicinal drug—used to cure diarrhea, mainly—to being used as a recreational narcotic. The number of users was in the millions. Government clerks, imperial eunuchs—no party was left free from the confines of opium, and recreational opium consumption was a practice considered characteristic of modernity and upper-class bourgeois culture. Nearly all of this opium was imported from Britain, from the East India Company which manufactured it in Bengal and licensed private traders to ship it to China11. By 1838, the amount of opium being privately imported to China was around 40,000 chests.

Opium, more than anything else, ended up being one of the primary catalysts for what the Chinese would later rechristen the ‘Century of Humiliation.’ By 1813, smoking opium was not only illegal, but punishable by law—100 lashes were guaranteed to anyone who would be caught smoking the product. Of course, opium was also vastly addictive, and to stop using it was to give oneself up to a vast number of physical withdrawal symptoms. In the words of politician Lin Zexu— one of the primary proponents of the ‘punish pushers’ approach to opium legislation in the mid-1800s—writing to Queen Victoria:

Formerly, smokers were few in number; but of late the contagion has spread, and its flowing poison has daily increased […] But ever since the great Ch'ing dynasty united the empire, its aim has been to regulate manners and customs with the view of rectifying the heart of man; how then can our House allow those who live within the girdle of the Seas to poison themselves at their own sweet will? Therefore, all who trade in or smoke opium in the Inner Land will be most severely punished, and the introduction and circulation of the drug will be for ever prohibited. It appears that this particular form of poison is illegally prepared by scoundrels in the tributary tribes of your honourable country and in the devil-regions under your jurisdiction; but of course it is neither prepared nor sold by your sovereign orders. Further, that it is not all nations but only some which prepare this article; and that you do not allow your own people to smoke, under severe penalties for disobedience, evidently knowing what a curse it is and therefore strictly prohibiting the practice. But better still than forbidding people to smoke, would it not be to forbid the sale and also the preparation of opium?

The opium situation in China eventually got so bad that an enormous amount of Chinese silver was being exchanged for opium, leading the kingdom to financial ruin—and by 1840 British commercial interests had grown so strong that they could only be managed by war. 20 years of alternating war and unequal ceasefire was followed by an 1860 regulation legalizing opium. By 1906, 25% of China’s male population was addicted to opium. Finally, legislation in 1906 began the long process of reversing the opium crisis, a process which was only brought to total completion with the reforms of Mao Zedong starting from 1949.

The whole process took 150 years.

The opium crisis remains one of the bedrocks of Chinese history and the national consciousness. The loss in the first Opium War against the British Empire destroyed the Chinese international position. It was one of the fundamental policy proposals that led to a turning point in the history of the Qing Empire, and the devastating effects of the opium mania are well-found throughout the annals of Chinese history.

In contrast, the social media arguably age started in 2007, with the launch of the iPhone. These ‘disruptive’ technologies proved not only to be the stalwarts of the history of global capitalism, but also enormously consequential to the generations that were raised on them—and despite warnings from as far back as 2008 that the infinite scroll would lead to mass losses in attention span and critical thinking abilities no attempts were made rid them of their addictive potential or of the effect they had on the human consciousness. All the prophecies of the social media detractors are now true: the average rates of reading and writing comprehension, along with IQ—flawed a measure as it is—are decreasing; the President is elected based on tiktok palatability rather than any kind of economic platform, unemployment continues to rise, the consolidation of the sources of production has never been more naked than before, and algorithmic advances and recommendation systems have led to widespread failure of the 20th century cultural systems—like always, capitalism is eating its own customers, having failed to see them as anything but units of production.

Of course, there have not been any Opium Wars, either, so it’s very possible that the ‘century of humiliation’ has, in fact, not yet begun—perhaps LLMs will prove to be the disrupter that ends the first ‘cycle’ of the internet, but hardly can anyone call them a superior replacement. It took 100 years after the Opium Wars for the crisis to end. It got worse before it got better. There will, inevitably, be a day that humans are free from the handcuffs of these technologies that seek to do little but sap away our freedom, free once again on the edge of the American frontier—but there may be a century-wide gulf of dystopia until that day arrives and we must ensure until that time that the lessons of the 21st century will not be long-forgotten, take all the opportunities we get to denounce and decry these oppressive tools that seek only to alienate us from ourselves, to dehumanize people and turn them into slovenly beasts of their own nature. If history tells us anything, it is that while the day of reckoning does eventually arrive, there is no limit to how bad things can get in the interim.

1

Taken from The Material Fall of Roman Britain, 300-525 CE, by Robin Fleming.

2

That said I think this is also not really much relief, because those problems could very well encompass your own lifespan and you’ll never really live to see the day that they get fixed—cold comfort in that. What I advocate for is a kind of understanding that things are bad and also understanding why they are bad and attempting to carve out the best you can do within the circumstances. Panicking doesn’t lead to much, you always gotta be on the up-dawg. We’re all going to make it…

3

Well okay it’s close insofar as ‘I’m pretty sure there’s going to be a major market correction within the next year or two,’ is close, though if you’re a wall street guy you’re going to want the actual quarter at the very least which is a lot trickier to get right. Of course it could also not be a bubble, but that would, again, require something historically unprecedented to happen, which of course could happen, don’t get me wrong, but it’s a lot easier for people to think that something historically unprecedented is happening than something historically unprecedented actually be happening.

4

I actually gave a talk about this a while ago at a socialist seminar, where I was kind of openly wondering if a socialist world even has cinema within it. Certainly one form of socialist world (hunter-gatherers) doesn’t.

5

I am really disappointed that these people are nerds. Politicians are pretty evil but it is nevertheless fun watching them whiz around doing utterly inane things—lots of Caligulas making their horse consul in the political sphere, but the techbros are doing things like somehow making smoking incredibly uncool. One wonders how they do it.

6

Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, Glass-Steagall act, JOBS act...

7

Actually what’s also crazy here is that Zuckerberg, despite ostensibly being the villain, is actually right: he unironically just is the town square and not the publisher, it’s not like he’s making any of the content on his platform. It’s a lot more dangerous for him to actively participate in regulation: really, one guy gets to decide everything I see on the internet?

8

I wonder what would an LLM look like that was trained only over pre-1960 data… wouldn’t it present an accurate summary of the shared human consciousness until that time (or at least of the literary cultures that had been well-represented up until that time)? No poisoned data from modern historical analysis—just a bonafide representation of the pre-1960 dataset. Perhaps when it spoke more elegantly we’d realize that indeed we are stupider than those people.

9

In the case of LLMs this is particularly interesting because people who develop ‘AI psychosis’ often start anthropomorphizing LLMs: one conversation with such people and you can immediately tell they are kind of vaguely ill and catastrophizing, their ideas about super-intelligences are deeply incoherent and rely on foundational assumptions that have no basis in wider human society.

10

There is also this talk of ‘the end of humanity,’ which I suppose is technically plausible but seems to assume either that all reasonable human beings have vanished off the face of the earth or that several things which seem like science fiction—like cold fusion—are not only possible but potentially monetarily profitable, which seems like a rather unprecedented jump in assumption. I suppose the best one can accomplish is something like ‘the Amish inherit the Earth.’

11

Most of this is from The Cambridge Illustrated History Of China, by Patricia Buckley Ebrey.

entry.title: ize of the world
entry.content:
I thought about both of them when I said to Saint-Laurent I wanted to make a film, just as Plisnier returned to his old love, revolutionary politics.

I wondered: “Could I make a film knowing how to make it now like I did, but also as if I was now transported to make a film like Melville had done when he made Le Silence de la mer?”

— Jean-Luc Godard

He wanted to get back to the old ways of making films, the ways he started out with, but with the distance of experience.

— Fabrice Aragno, on Godard

One of the reasons it is difficult to write about Godard is because it is difficult to know what Godard you are referring to. Is it the flashy Godard of the early years, the storyteller, the Godard so full of joie de vivre? Is it the political Godard of the ‘70s, estranged from his community and the people of his homeland? The more conventional return to form, the experimental sentimentality of Historie(s) or Eloge de l’amour? The late-period essayist? The number of iterations Godard cycled through were so multitudinous, so vibrant, that pinning him down as anything but a master of the visual form is close to impossible; his union with the moving image was so foundational to his being that it is hardly possible to imagine anyone who fundamentally knew more about what cinema was, is and will continue to be. This was a man whose very thought proceeded in images.

I watched a Godard at Berkeley the other day at a special BAMPFA screening. To my right were two old French women I had a little chat with in my own broken recitation of their language; they were thoroughly amused, but encouraging nevertheless. The film was Bande à part. I was hungry and frustrated—a tram derail and a slow cheeseburger order had left me in a poor mood, overall, but all that business vanished from my mind the moment that Anna Karina’s face entered the image. It is hard to watch a film, especially one as joyous as this, and not find yourself far from the roiling crowds of despair and the prophets of your ruin but rather in, in true Sherlock Jr. fashion—a film that I now know was deeply loved by Godard, so bare are its influences in Bande à part—into the throes of the past. And yet even as you are there, transfixed, you can find a deep and fundamental joy in their hearts that is so unwilling to find itself a place within your own.

They made Casablanca in 1942. There was a war—the very worst—and they, in turn, responded with Casablanca. How could that be? How could those people—the very same species, people not very different from us, not far removed either in space or time—how could those people see the unending death and devastation around them and respond with a movie so relentless in its thirst for honor and devotion, so uniquely committed to love and duty? How could they find it in themselves to care so, so much?

The truth is that no matter what Godard you care to discuss that common strand uniting all his iterations never failed—the strand that held nothing but care and utmost respect for cinema and its masters, and knew, deep down, that it was worth trying to make something new out of film, not because it was easy, but because it was hard.

not because it is easy, but because it is hard

I suppose at this point mathematicians are in something not far from shambles. ‘Gradually, and then suddenly’—so says Mike Campbell about the arrival of his bankruptcy in Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises, and the quote is perhaps one of those rare generalities that can apply to any number of situations. It is also one that is apt for this particular course of affairs—the plague of LLMs in mathematics, and the deluge of automation that is following. Until this June I had never even seen a mathematician using LLMs to make novel discoveries in his field. Then suddenly it is October and I can see all my favorite open problems falling, uniformly, like dominoes. There is some sense in which this was inevitable, and about a month ago I placed a bet with a good friend that such a thing would occur on timescales not very far from those we have already hit today1. That particular bet has not been collected—not yet, anyway—but my moral preparation for living in a world inhabited not by mathematicians, but by buttons which when pressed reveal the infinitude of mathematical truth has more-or-less reached completion. The method in which this manifests is a profound numbness. In fact I have never been more keenly aware that in a rather meaningful sense these solutions are, ultimately, just a bunch of words on a page. That they carry profound insight in them is a function not of their inherent worth, but of the hairless apes that devised them, and those who cared enough to factory-line them.

How odd to think so! It seems that I must welcome such a renaissance of mathematical knowledge, and yet all I feel is apathy. In fact I very much do not seem to care about the whole business at all, beyond the occasional flicker at the manner of result. One can say that I am disappointed in God—not because of this whole business that only other humans, not He, has wrought, and undoubtedly forms part of the grand, cosmic plan He has for all of us—for allowing there to exist a $n(\log n)^{1-2^{-182}}$ algorithm for integer multiplication2, but that truly is, these days, secondary. By and large the whole business feels very much inconsequential. So be it, then, let them put up whatever number of papers they want. When the ‘all at once’ does arrive—in consequential terms, as in, if I get laid off, or if some sort of catastrophe occurs—it will arrive, and there is little that can be done about it.

I suspect in many ways this sounds to the uninformed like a form of denial. Admittedly it would be good to have a little bit of denial—but then again, the cat is out of the bag, and it is quite a perilous cat that people have unleashed, even if it never really gains any further capabilities beyond solving mathematical problems at all, and attempting to deny this fact does not make it go away. But what can come off as denial is only a natural response to a profound question of meaning. I have been, at various times over the last few months, chastised for being rather gloomy in the face of what appears to be ‘progress.’ Surely more is better, right? Do the great mathematical minds of the world not want this? Is this not what they desired—that their problems be solved? Besides the usual arguments about adapting3 and progress for progress’ sake, the one I am faced with the most is this bizarre fixation on democratization and skillset transfer: that in truth this lowers the barrier of entry into mathematics, and now anyone can make a novel contribution. Isn’t that great?

And indeed it is tempting to think so. But one of the problems of interacting with people who are limited in their understanding of mathematics is that they know little of what they are indeed missing out on. And while I may sound accusatory or dismissive, the reason they know little of what they are missing out on is precisely because they do not know mathematics.

knowledge and wisdom

I dislike quoting from the internet, but these unprecedented times call for unprecedented measures. Here is a sentiment I saw expressed on Substack the other day:

When I tell you that AI has utterly ruined my job, it is an understatement. Teaching writing to students who see no value in the skill, and consequently no value in what I offer them is just torturous. What used to be a collegial, fun engagement is now just an exercise in adversarial one-upping. Exhausting to lose every skill and sensibility one has worked for over three decades.

It is hard not to pity the woman who wrote this: to see some of the things you care about so deeply discarded by the wayside due to simple economics, and to see the generational tide turn in a rather ugly way. The kids do not know how to write, nor do they care how to write. They are college students—surely they must be interested in their own mental development, in their intellectual flourishing? How could they do this if they do not know how to write?

The answer, of course, seems to be the same as that of why they don’t do anything these days: writing is not an activity which can lead them to a materially successful life, and therefore there is little reason to pay to do it. This is a hard pill to swallow, but it is also not unprecedented. Certainly people do not go to school for artisanship en masse, not now that there are factories to create goods—there are factories to create writing, now, too, and so one does not need to be able to do it to be employed. But wondering if one needs to learn how to write in these days is not particularly different than wondering if one needs to learn how to do mathematics: it seems like the computer can do it, really, and therefore it’s unclear how valuable it is to learn. And there has always been truth to this. For the vast majority of human history, the masses were illiterate. Reading and writing was not the profoundly valuable skill it is today; indeed it was a skill cultivated by monks and intellectuals, and even when writing began arriving to the masses post the industrial revolution the actual act of literature being something that anyone—not just the English nobility, for instance—could partake in took even longer. Today you can go to college and get a degree in writing, just as you can go to college and get a degree in mathematics. In that sense what we appear to be going towards is a post-literate society.

Of course, one can hardly argue that not knowing writing and mathematics does not lead to mental decline.

Because isn’t that the goal? It seems on some fundamental level important that we as a society progress towards those ideals of antiquity that are so beloved to us: a vast and educated citizenry presided over by philosopher-kings, where each man partakes in his own manner of intellectual and physical flourishing. A society comprised of healthy and resilient men and women that consists of partaking in art and pleasure, where each person knows their duty to society and carries it out obediently not out of force but out of their own wise choice. Such a society is utopian and may ultimately even be contrary to human nature, but it is a worthwhile goal nevertheless. And yet it so occurs that the children do not want to learn how to write. Their objection is the same as that of mathematics: why? Why do it when a computer can do it? How does addition help me if we live in a world with a calculator?

It is only natural to ask these questions. Teachers, of course, respond with various pragmatisms, but telling a child who does not know writing and mathematics these answers is like trying to stuff the whole world into a telescope. In truth the answer is the same as it has ever been, to treat children like children and do unto them what they did unto all those who had similar objections a hundred years ago: make them eat their veggies. Perhaps attempting to convince them that these things are important is not just a failing activity, but it is something actively detrimental to their well-being: are things only good if their obvious benefits can be laid bare in material fashion right down on the blackboard? There is no choice in the matter—perhaps ‘you must do it because I said you must’ is good enough of an answer? To explain to someone who does not know how to write the obvious benefits of knowing how to write—the way it organizes your thoughts, the way it transforms your rhetoric, the ability it gives you to parse increasingly complex inner frameworks, the way it allows for far superior communication ability—is indeed difficult, because the skills required to understand what knowing how to write does for a person are precisely those which are present only in those who do, indeed, know how to write.

It is most certainly a curious state of affairs. But then so are all such matters concerned with the transference of wisdom.

One of the reasons I talk about writing so much while thinking of mathematics is because those things, to me, do not seem unrelated. There are many who will point out that there is a certain skill in the presentation and writing of mathematical results on its own—a phrase widely touted and even a major objective of study among the mathematicians of old, who really were very concerned with what ‘proof’ and ‘truth’ really entailed, but generally discarded in practice by the working mathematician, who favors complex problem-solving over presentation. There are many strange reasons why this is the case. The classical one, of course, has to do with the fact that academia presents an optimization problem—it carries within itself its own currency, one of prestige, and the way to succeed in that game is to gain the recognition of one’s peers. More pragmatically, this currency forms the basis of hiring decisions, and one’s peers of course heavily value those who contribute to the opus of human knowledge through solving harder and harder problems and making increasing amounts of breakthroughs over presenting a few problems well. This is only natural. But there is a certain art to presenting mathematics, and it is one that is baked into its culture by the nature of its beings. Why do mathematicians have their own lingo? The colloquial usage of terms like ‘trivial’ and ‘epsilon probability’ follows from their extraordinary ability to describe phenomena—even beyond mathematical—with great precision. This phenomenon of understanding the preciseness of your rhetoric is one that has great overlap between mathematics and writing. To write is to distill the essence of one’s disorganized and, frankly, irrational means of thought into a continuous series of words that betray the essence of the idea to anyone who chooses to gaze upon it. So is mathematical proof. The way that intellectual thought organizes itself into rhetorical arguments is the same way that mathematical feeling and intuition organizes itself into the concreteness of lemma-arguments and theorem statements. And, much like writing, the only way people can get better at mathematics is by doing mathematics. The wisdom gained therein from deep mathematical thought is a curious sort of wisdom that is quite divorced from that of mere knowledge.

If one reads widely and deliberately one inordinately begins to draw directions between seemingly unrelated things and starts seeing the essential patterns among them, and one who does mathematics, can, too, start to understand various phenomena with much intensity. To give my own embarrassing example, my group theory class in undergrad was well-motivated, and for a long time the professor made us write down long tables of groups such as $Q_8$ or $A_4$, along with painstakingly listing the actions from the group to itself. It seemed like a profoundly boring exercise, not dissimilar to learning your times-tables. But understanding the structure of these groups indeed has an effect not very different from that of your times-tables: the ability to multiply numbers at will indeed has quite a strong effect on anyone doing higher mathematics, at least as an endless source of examples and tests and deep understanding of those numbers. Similarly, knowing $Q_8$ like an old friend provides you with the ability to reason about groups at deep levels and learn much more context about the levels you are operating on. Here is a ‘thought’ I had about a year or two after that class:

The Sylow theorems are a partial converse to Lagrange’s theorem.

Many would find this statement obvious, or entirely trivial. But I arrived at this conclusion precisely while attempting to answer a question about groups; indeed I had essentially forgotten what the Sylow theorems were, and it was a last-ditch attempt to throw large-scale machinery at the problem in the hopes of arriving at something from it. So I looked them up, and the above thought struck me. I knew that there was in fact no complete converse to Lagrange’s theorem because I had an intuitive knowledge of my pesky friend $A_4$, and so when I understood that the Sylow theorems formed a partially successful attempt to construct that converse my understanding of them suddenly become far deeper—in the past I had not even remembered the statement, but this flash of understanding allowed me to derive the proof of the first theorem entirely on my own. There are many components to this knowledge; that converses are desirable on their own, for instance, which someone has to have encountered via attempts to solve a problem to realize the generality of, or that even a partial converse can prove useful, or why only a partial converse succeeds in this setting—not merely because of the existence of a counterexample in $A_4$ but the fundamental structure of $A_4$ that prevents the existence of one (and indeed, exploiting such structures is how one arrives at the proof).

This kind of deep, structural knowledge of mathematics is something that is easy to approximate but difficult to communicate. It is an exercise in mathematical wisdom that allows one to grasp the essential quality of the structures one is dealing with. The problem is that a single read-through of a textbook does not provide one with this knowledge, even if one is able to solve the occasional problem using it (and indeed solving the occasional problem is exactly how universities and schools attempt to teach mathematics—it is not the most optimal solution, perhaps, but it is about the best that can be done). It arrives when it arrives.

the devil of gratification

Commercial mathematics does not reward deep work. Commercial writing does, sometimes—it is similarly a skill to develop writing, and often many insightful ideas are unlocked within the process of writing itself, knowing that what you are writing is in some sense ‘good’ and that feeling of clicking together—but the vast majority of writing is for minor reasons. Not bad reasons, per se, but minor reasons—writing a text, for instance, or writing an email. Most people these days do not write more than that.

But the act of understanding mathematics is such a personal and intimate one that it does not seem to have much in the way of material reward at all. Nevertheless, it is both very difficult and very easy indeed to communicate why that activity is worth doing, and is probably summarized by my favorite Seinfeld quote of all time:

George: Why would I spend seven dollars to see a movie that I could watch on TV?

Kramer: Well, why go to a fine restaurant, when you can just stick something in the microwave? Why go to the park and fly a kite, when you can just pop a pill?

In truth, the rewards of activities are only the essential fundamentals about them that can be garnered through an amount of wisdom that is inculcated by those who do the activity as a being unto itself. There are many who run long-distances, but the true long-distance runner is not the one who runs the longest, but the one who runs solely for for its own sake4, and not to present to the world that one is a runner. There are scruffily-dressed Frenchmen that run miles in four minutes and stop for smoke breaks after each fifth that can outrun steady trainers, not because they have it in them this optimal desire for improvement, but because to them the activity is merely the activity. That is not to say they don’t have a desire for improvement—it is simply secondary to doing the activity. Magnus Carlsen worked hard, but he did not work hard because he wanted to show to everyone that he was the best at chess, nor did he work optimally, nor did he play the perfect games. He simply loved Chess too much to not. So is true about Michael Jordan, and so is true about Paul McCartney, and so is true about Alexander Grothendeick. And so is true about the old men who sit under the trees of the Jardin du Luxembourg and play chess—not because they want to be the best but because they love the game, and because they possess the insightful wisdom of those who have dedicated themselves to it. Indeed, listen to then watch games between genius prodigies. Their appreciation and understanding operates on a level far beyond that of the competitor.

What I say is banal, but what I say is also fundamentally human. What are we doing if we are not trying to achieve human transcendence? The ability to be lost in the playing of guitar, to experience runner’s high, to be locked into a sweaty game with a rival, to find oneself mesmerized by the beauty of the Nullstellansatz—is that not what being human is all about?

And then one wonders why those who feel this intimate sublimity of the human experience resist the loss of their communities in the face of ‘progress.’

Of course, there is no one more dangerous in that regard than one who devalues this foundational experience of humanity in favor of playing God. It is fun to play God, but that fun quickly gets boring, just as it is fun to eat nothing but pizza at first until on the fifth day you realize you have turned quite sickly indeed, and the thought of putting another slice in your mouth fills you with horror, and you realize that even the old head of broccoli that you so despised now looks profoundly appealing in the face of this fatty sludge. To say that you are doing mathematics by pressing buttons certainly can provide that little piece of pleasure that pizza does, but without the deep understanding of mathematical wisdom it becomes an experience scarcely different from pressing a button on a jack-in-the-box and watching the clown pop out—fun at first, but ultimately meaningless. There is only meaning to endeavors insofar as humans do them, just as there is only meaning to art insofar as humans make it.

In short, the difficult question of whether mathematics survives this assault is one that, to me, has a simple answer: times of abundance are times of decadence, and the act of doing mathematics is only meaningful in the midst of being unable to do it. We are a decadent generation, so prone to enriching our material selves that we forget what it is to do things slow and with patience and with profound and transformative love for the thing in and of itself, the ding an sich, so prone to acquiring the cheap thrills of ‘understanding’ through watching videos and ignoring the touch of wise teachers and great thinkers, so conceited, in fact, that we forget that despite all the essentials of technology the only way to ever truly learn mathematics is the way it has always been—alone on a table with a pencil and a paper in hand, perhaps a book, deciphering the enigmatic texts within and gaining the deep knowledge of generations past. One may dislike doing so. One may even despise it—but that is okay, for it is not easy to gain this wisdom, and it really is only by sailing across the long ocean that one can arrive at the promised land. There truly are no shortcuts, and if one has been taken, you can rest assured that it is not Eden that you have arrived at but afar from your path onto Calypso’s isle where eating the lotuses will never ease your longing for the shore.

And you can go on again and again and again refining and even rebelling against the wisdom of the ancients, but time and again their words prove prescient beyond all recognition:

It is not the destination that is the point, but the journey.

All so many words for a lesson so short, yet a lesson that we as humans are so painstakingly wont to discard that we may yet forget that Godard quote all the way at the beginning, the words of a dying man as he remembered the follies of his youth and determined that what he loved, more than anything, was the film, the motion picture as-is, and after all his years of understanding and developing the taste for cinema that so defined his own career he realized that there was nothing he wanted more than to make a simple, a basic film, one not so different from Le Silence de la Mer—a film for people and about people, a film about love and hope, a film that preceded the entirety of his own ambitions. ‘The old ways of making films’—perhaps the only ones.

1

Alas, time passes. We often wish that it wouldn’t, but then that is one those pesky little inevitabilities that make us care about time in the first place.

2

Though no doubt that He is good and it is simply an intermediate on our path to discovering the $n\sqrt{\log n}$ or $n\log\log n$ bounds.

3

Generally ludicrous: to anyone even mildly capable the ‘adaptation’ here is next to trivial, and ultimately the goal of these people is to eliminate any form of adaptivity in the first place; they quite explicitly desire full replacement. In any case, such arguments fall apart very quickly—we should attempt to become mathematical expositors, but then exposition is something AI can do better than us (it can’t), we should attempt to do x but then AI can also do x, blah blah blah; just automation, really.

4

Perhaps not coincidentally at the highest echelons these people tend the one and the same—to be truly great at something you must do that something for its own sake, and not to be great at it. Greatness is happenstance.

entry.title: and so we find ourselves here again where it all started
entry.content:
One of the things that is so slippery and yet evocative about the work of David Foster Wallace is that when he attempts to address the psychology of people who have been exposed to modernity he often addresses their psychologies as a whole, whatever that comprises of, and sometimes his attempt to address these psychologies comes off sounding much less diagnostic and clinical and closer to what can be perceived as cruel. It is true that Wallace is often cruel, and it is true that Wallace is often clinical. But in that sense his batting average with respect to only subjecting those who are actually deserving of his mirth to it is quite high, even if it takes a little bit of time to actually perceive it as so—which happened to me with his short story The Depressed Person, one that I categorically rejected the first time I encountered it on qualms of it being far too uncomfortable of an experience to actually flip through, but which since then I have periodically revisited until now when reading it is nearly always a transformative experience. Like most of Wallace’s work, it feels like it has the secrets of the universe hidden within it.1

I guess what takes a while to actually understand and internalize about The Depressed Person is that it requires you to sit with a rather uncomfortable truth that, like a lot of Wallace’s work, is then reflected back on the reader instead of the head of the person we are currently inhabiting—who, in this case, turns out to be depressed, for some measure of depressed. Because it is called The Depressed Person you’d like to think that the story is about depression, but it really isn’t, despite the fact that it does often form the same kind of projection exercise that Good Old Neon does. I think of myself as very much like Neal from Good Old Neon; I even phrase things the same way he does, in his unique blend of preppy and regular-guy lowbrow, but unlike him it the accusations and feeling of being a fraud—or really what’s more like a fundamental inability to inhabit the world you are in now, instead of perceiving things via this third person perspective of someone who is judging the person you are within the body that you inhabit, you who can’t even lose yourself within the arms of the pretty girl at school because you’re so neurotic about being the person who finally found himself within those said arms—that feeling of being a fraud is something that I know all-too-well but unlike Neal does not cause me any kind of discomfort, it’s just there, present, ‘coolio isn’t it great that she’s right here next to me, that I’m the guy who’s in her arms’ without the aforementioned sadness that I’m thinking that instead of fully experiencing or being in the moment, whatever that means. I could lament not being in the moment, but after all, I am simply myself and can’t be anyone else, no matter how hard I may try, so not-really-being-in-the-moment is just something that I do, and that is what comprises being-in-the-moment for me after all. There’s a lot more processing there than just that simple aphorism; I’m sure there are quite a number of clicks and wires going off in that brain of mine, but whenever that happens it doesn’t hit the ‘and I hate myself for it’ part of the brain and so I can read Good Old Neon and feel seen and experience a kind of catharsis despite not finding myself looking for a toilet bowl to puke in midway through because I saw something I didn’t like in those pages.

The Depressed Person is a bit more like that. As I said, I didn’t like it at first. It was painful and bewildering to read precisely because the usual writerly empathy that Wallace gives to Kate Gompert and her desire to jump off a burning building in Infinite Jest is absent and replaced with almost a sneering, wallowing sense of cruelty. Wallace, it seems, does not actually like the depressed person, even as he obviously feels some sense of pity towards her.

It is hard to reconcile these two things, at least for me. It is easy to me to empathize with the depressed person, not only because I have experienced several of those emotions firsthand off-and-on during various times of my life but also because he includes several of those little tidbits that serve to humanize someone by presenting episodes of their life in a manner that makes you feel a kind of pitiable sadness inside, the kind of empathy you feel when you hear about a little boy who invited his whole class to his birthday party and sat at the table with his hat and balloons and the hours ticking by while the slow realization that no one was going to arrive creeped upon him. The depressed person’s parents got divorced and they wouldn’t even buy her retainers, for instance, and when they did it was some kind of divorce-related power play. What kind of an effect that would have on a young girl!

Stories like those, in isolation, can paint the picture of someone who has been subjected repeatedly to negative experiences in their life leading to what psychologists call ‘accumulated trauma.’ Because Wallace is writing about modernity, he is interested in the way that ‘accumulated trauma’ manifests in modernity, with all the nice techniques and gizmos we have to thoroughly psychoanalyze ourselves and understand, of course, that the source of our traumas are often rooted in the fundamental aspects of our childhood, and that addressing their ‘root causes’ involves quite a great deal of back-and-forth with professionals that help you better understand how to deal with the behaviors you have imbibed by these traumas. Whenever I think of things like this it reminds me of a story that an old friend of my dad’s told me while digging through a stash of boxes in his garage during a clean-up drive. One of the boxes sidelined at the very end contained some of his effects from when he was a high-school boy, all the way back in rural India, and they contained a hefty number of comic books along with several illustrations he himself had made which were quite sophisticated for a high school boy and wove themselves into coherent and funny storylines. I asked him if he used to make comics as a kid. There was the familiar wonder in his eyes of a man recollecting fond memories that had not been summoned for almost as long a period as had passed since their formation. Then he laughed and told me about how he used to draw these all the time back in ninth or tenth grade and how sometimes the kids used to make fun of him, going so far as to even tear a few of his preciously made comics and throw them into the trash. It was quite a horrible little memory, and for a second I did not really know what was coming next. Then he threw his head back and laughed widely, as if it were something really funny, and when I asked him if he had stopped after that he said hell no, he didn’t even remember who the boys were and had simply glued them together and finally only stopped drawing them the next year after his interest petered out.

What I’m trying to get at is that it’s kind of amazing to me that he laughed.

In retrospect it shouldn’t be. But then we live in a world driven by ressentiment and seeing people who are so obviously free of the things that burden several of those among us is kind of a surreal experience. It feels hard to imagine that a person who has obviously been subjected to what by definition is a kind of childhood traumatic experience can laugh so freely about it while being entirely unaffected by an episode that by any psychoanalytic measure should have been imprinted upon his psyche along with innumerable other such reinforcing experiences that serve only to erode his self-esteem.

Or rather what I’m getting at is that the depressed person’s depression stemmed from a fundamental accumulation of such psychoanalytic traumas that it basically rendered her incapable of doing anything because she was caught up in her head about said traumas.
